blocks.text: Where rendering fits
What a mesh is: vertices, edges, faces
UVs and materials
PBR: the three judgments
Lights and shadows
What the lab will build
A rendered frame is the end of a chain: mesh defines the shape, material defines how light interacts with the surface, lights define where the light comes from, and the camera decides what you see.
This week is about the first three.
The lab will put them together in one small studio, but today is the theory that lets you judge whether the result looks right.

slides.title: What Is a Mesh? Vertices, Edges, and Faces

blocks.text: A mesh is a collection of connected geometry:
A vertex (plural: vertices) is a point in 3D space
An edge is a line between two vertices
A face is a closed loop of edges; in real-time rendering it is almost always a triangle
A polygon is a face with more than three sides; the GPU splits it into triangles before drawing
The wireframe view shows edges and faces without materials — it is how you inspect the structure
A cube has 8 corners but 24 vertices in Unity, because each face needs its own normal and UV data
Triangles are the GPU's native primitive:
Every quad, polygon, or imported model is triangulated before rendering
A normal is the direction a face points; it tells the light how to shade the surface
Flat shading uses one normal per face — hard edges
Smooth shading shares averaged normals across vertices — soft, rounded edges
If a model looks faceted when it should be smooth, the normals are the first thing to check
You do not need to memorise vertex counts; you need to know that geometry and normals are separate data
A UV is a 2D coordinate that maps a texture onto a 3D surface:
U is horizontal, V is vertical; the range is normally 0 to 1
Each vertex stores a UV coordinate, so the texture knows which part of the image belongs to which triangle
Tiling repeats the texture; offset shifts it; seams appear where UV islands are cut apart
A UV map is the bridge between a flat image and a curved surface
If a texture looks stretched or upside down, the UVs — not the material — are usually the cause
A Material is an asset that binds a shader and its parameter values:
The shader is the recipe — it decides how the surface responds to light
The parameters are the ingredients — colour, metallic, smoothness, textures
The MeshRenderer holds a reference to the material and draws it
Several objects can share one material; changing the asset updates all of them
A per-renderer override is possible, but start with shared materials
In URP, use URP/Lit; the Built-in Standard shader in a URP project turns materials pink
Most "ugly materials" come from three PBR values:
Albedo (base colour) — the surface colour, not a paint layer; use a real reference
Metallic — 0 for wood, plastic, glass, skin; 1 for metal. Do not use 0.5 unless you know why
Smoothness — 0 is matte, 1 is a mirror; a dielectric with high smoothness looks like plastic
Normal map — a texture that adds surface detail without adding geometry; it must be imported as Normal map, not Default
For metals, albedo is the reflection tint: gold is yellow, copper is orange, silver is white
If a surface looks wrong, check these four before anything else
These are the three materials the lab will build. Read them as expected results, not as a live build:
Metal — metallic 1, smoothness 0.9, albedo #888888; a sharp highlight that takes the light's colour
Wood — metallic 0, smoothness 0.2, albedo #8B5A2B; a broad, soft highlight and a matte surface
Glass — metallic 0, smoothness 1, Surface Type Transparent, alpha 0.3; the background shows through
All three sit under the same directional light; the same light produces three different surfaces
When you build them in the lab, change one slider at a time and compare against this reference
Four failures to recognise on sight:
Normal map imported as Default — the surface looks flat from the side; set Texture Type to Normal map
Smoothness too high on wood — everything looks wet or plastic; lower it to 0.2–0.3
Built-in Standard shader in a URP project — the material turns pink; recreate it with URP/Lit
Albedo used as paint on a metal — the metal looks dull and off-colour; use the real metal colour
AI can suggest a value, but it cannot see the result. The check is visual, in Play Mode
Directional — parallel rays, like the sun.
No position, only rotation and colour; affects the whole scene. Point — a bulb.
Has position, range, colour; falls off with distance. Spot — a flashlight.
Has position, direction, angle, range; falls off with distance and angle.
Use soft shadows on the directional, and turn shadows off on point and spot lights unless you need them.
Realtime — rendered every frame; needed for moving lights and objects; expensive
Baked — pre-computed into a lightmap; static objects only; free at runtime
Mixed — dynamic objects cast realtime shadows into baked areas
The light's Mode setting chooses Realtime, Baked, or Mixed
If a light or its objects never move, bake it — it saves GPU and often looks better
In the lab you will build one scene, Lab8_MaterialsLights:
A metal cube, a wood sphere, and a glass capsule
One Directional, one Point, and one Spot light
You will author each material by hand, verify it in Play Mode, and compare the three falloff behaviours
You will also debug a broken scene with four hidden material/lighting bugs
Nothing is submitted after class — you will demo the finished scene to your neighbour and the TA in the room
A mesh is vertices, edges, and faces; triangles are the GPU's native primitive
Normals control shading; UVs map a 2D texture onto a 3D surface
A material binds a shader and parameters; PBR is albedo, metallic, and smoothness
Directional, Point, and Spot lights have different falloff; bake static lights
